newsitem.title: USA: Rifkind warns of conflict if NATO doesn't expand.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind warns of conflict if NATO doesn't expand.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind warned on Monday that Europe could be plunged into fresh ethnic and nationalistic conflict if Russia succeeded in blocking NATO's plans for expansion.

In a speech to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, he said that unless the 16-nation alliance accepted new members, former Soviet allies in Eastern Europe would be cut off by a new Iron Curtain descending over the continent.

"They would have to make their own security arrangements, independent of the countries to their west whose interests and values they share," he said. "Local and regional alliances would spring up in a frightening facsimile of pre-Second World War Europe."

"There could be new tremors along ethnic and nationalistic faultlines," he said. "A dismal prospect indeed and one that could easily draw us in Western Europe and America into new tension and conflict."

Moscow has long opposed NATO enlargement on the grounds that it endangers Russia's security, but the alliance insists that it intends at a July summit in Madrid to invite several former Warsaw Pact states to start talks on membership.
Rifkind was clearly responding to a growing number of editorials and commentaries in the U.S. press opposing the Clinton administration's drive for NATO expansion.

He told reporters at a breakfast meeting that he welcomed the enlargement debate, but said: "We should respond to that, explain why enlargement can entirely be justified in terms of European security."

In his speech, Rifkind said NATO was doing its best to reassure Moscow it had no intention of launching an assault and also spelled out the risks if countries like Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary were not admitted to NATO.

"First, the countries of Central Europe would conclude that they remained in Russia's sphere of influence. The steady, predictable strategy of enlargement that has been set for three years would have been halted in its tracks, just because Russia did not like it. I can scarcely imagine the consequences in Central Europe," he said.

"If the process were to be stopped altogether, they would be forced to adopt national rather than cooperative defence strategies," said Rifkind, in Washington for talks with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen and members of Congress.

"We would have a line down the middle of Europe, just like the Iron Curtain, with only Eastern Germany having moved from one side to the other. The Iron Curtain was a cruel aberration. It cannot be right to perpetuate its divisions in any form," he said.

Rifkind rejected arguments put forward by critics that NATO could not enlarge while simultaneously building a new relationship with Russia, saying Moscow could only benefit from security on its western borders.

"It faces uncertainty to its south, with a number of bitter conflicts close to its border. In the east, Russia has to reckon with a rising China and guard against events in the unpredictable North Korea -- also, let us not forget, on Russia's border," he said.
"A sure peace with the West is a godsent opportunity for Russia, and (her) leaders know that," he said.
NATO is offering Moscow a voice in the alliance's deliberations but no right of veto. The two sides are now trying to negotiate a charter to govern future relations.
Moscow said on Sunday that talks between Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana had been "positive" but differences remained.
